analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent and repeals the individual alternative minimum tax.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. Jon Kyl with 25 Republican cosponsors, the bill sat in the Senate Finance Committee for the rest of the 110th Congress and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would lock in the Bush-era tax cuts permanently by removing their expiration dates: lower income tax rates, full repeal of the estate tax, and the reduced tax rates on dividends and capital gains [S2][S3]. It would also make permanent the research tax credit, the small-business expensing allowance, and the school-teacher expense deduction, and it would repeal the individual alternative minimum tax after 2006 [S2][S3]. A final section merely expresses the Senate's view that tax reform legislation should be written, which changes nothing by itself [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most: permanent repeal of the estate tax benefits the largest estates, and the permanent lower rates on dividends and capital gains flow mainly to households that own stocks and other assets [S2][S3]. Corporations and research-intensive industries gain a permanent research credit instead of one that must be renewed every year or two [S2][S3]. Small businesses gain certainty from a permanent expensing allowance, and middle-income taxpayers who get caught by the alternative minimum tax would be freed from it [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 2010 expiration date of the 2001 tax law, making its lower income tax rates and full repeal of the estate and gift tax permanent [S2][S3].
Makes the reduced tax rates on dividends and capital gains from the 2003 tax law permanent, a benefit concentrated among households that own taxable investments [S2][S3].

Repeals the individual alternative minimum tax for tax years after 2006, relieving millions of mostly middle- and upper-middle-income taxpayers of a parallel tax system originally aimed at the very rich [S2][S3].
Makes permanent the research credit and the small-business expensing allowance (raised from $25,000 to $100,000), giving businesses a tax break that otherwise had to be repeatedly renewed [S2][S3].
Makes permanent the above-the-line deduction for elementary and secondary school teachers' out-of-pocket classroom expenses [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: No offsetting revenue is provided, so the cost of making all the tax reductions permanent would show up as larger federal deficits, borne by future taxpayers, or would have to be made up later through spending cuts or tax increases elsewhere [S2][S3]. Because the largest provisions — estate tax repeal and the capital gains and dividend rate cuts — concentrate their benefits at the top of the income scale while the cost is spread across everyone who pays for the debt, the average taxpayer pays more in the long run than the value of the cuts they personally receive [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Making every provision of the 2001 and 2003 tax laws permanent, plus repealing the individual AMT, would remove hundreds of billions of dollars per decade from federal revenue with no offset, increasing deficits and shifting the cost to future taxpayers [S2][S3].

The benefits are skewed toward the top: estate tax repeal affects only the largest estates, and the dividend and capital gains rate cuts flow disproportionately to high-income households that hold most taxable investment assets [S2][S3].

An honest supporter would concede that a permanent research credit and expensing allowance reward activities companies were already doing, and that the bill's 'sense of the Senate' on tax simplification is aspirational language that obligates no one [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some pieces are genuinely useful: repealing the AMT fixes a real problem for millions of families, and permanent expensing and the teacher deduction are modest, sensible provisions. But the bill's center of gravity — permanent estate tax repeal and permanent low rates on dividends and capital gains — delivers its largest benefits to the wealthiest households and adds substantially to the deficit with no pay-for. As a package, the long-run cost to ordinary taxpayers through debt and future fiscal pressure outweighs the broadly shared benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2007, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never reported out or brought to the floor before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Kyl and 22 other Republican senators introduced the bill on April 17, 2007, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S3][S5].
The bill attracted 25 Republican cosponsors in total, but no Democratic cosponsor [S4].
The Senate Finance Committee took no further action on the bill; the legislative record shows no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote [S1][S5].
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Future taxpayers are better off, since hundreds of billions in revenue over the following decade were not permanently removed. The estate tax and the current rates on capital gains and dividends also remained in place beyond 2010, so the tax code continued to collect from the largest estates and from investment income.

for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor; his committee held jurisdiction over the bill [S3].

for.name: Senate Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 25 cosponsors were Republicans [S4].

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Max Baucus (D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: no markup, no report, no vote was ever scheduled during the two-year Congress [S1][S5].

against.name: Senate Democratic majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate agenda in the 110th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with a Democratic majority and no Democratic cosponsors, the bill received no floor consideration [S1][S4][S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; no Democrat signed on, and a Democratic-controlled Senate never acted on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: Permanent estate tax repeal would benefit only the largest estates, and permanent low rates on dividends and capital gains flow mainly to households with significant investment income [S2][S3]. The revenue cost would be spread across everyone else through larger deficits [S2][S3].

A permanent research credit replaces a credit that lapses every year or two, giving companies a reliable, permanent tax reduction [S2][S3]. It is intended to encourage research spending that may benefit the public, but its cost lands on the general taxpayer.
Permanently raising the expensing allowance to $100,000 (with software eligible) lets small businesses deduct equipment costs immediately rather than over years [S2][S3].
